title: A Process's Memory: Segments, Storage Duration, and Lifetime
summary: Map the segments of a running program, watch objects of each storage duration being made and destroyed, and see where the stack and heap get memory.
intro: *How a Computer Runs Your Program* named three places a value can live: the stack, the heap, and static storage. *The Stack, the Heap, new and delete* worked with the first two. A running program has more regions than that. Its machine code, its string literals, and its globals each have a place of their own, and every object has a **storage duration** that decides when it's made and when it's destroyed. This lesson maps the whole layout with real tools, watches objects come and go, fixes a startup bug that depends on the order files are linked in, and follows `new` down to the kernel.

steps.title: The segments of a process
steps.body:
When you run a program, the kernel makes a **process** for it and the loader maps the executable into it. The process has its own **virtual address space**: the addresses its pointers hold belong to it alone, and no other program sees them. The next lesson shows how the OS maps them onto real memory. The compiler and the linker sort everything your program holds into **segments**, and the loader puts each one in its own region, lowest addresses first. Static storage, from *How a Computer Runs Your Program*, is really three of them, rodata, data, and bss:

| Segment | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| text | the machine code of every function |
| rodata | read-only data: string literals, `const` tables |
| data | globals and statics that start with a value |
| bss | globals and statics that start at zero |
| heap | what `new` and `malloc` hand out, growing up |
| stack | function frames, growing down from near the top |

Here is this part's example built on the Mac and measured by `size -m`, which lists each segment and its sections, and `nm`, the symbol table from *Headers, Translation Units, and the Linker*:

```text
$ size -m segments
Segment __PAGEZERO: 4294967296 (zero fill)
Segment __TEXT: 16384
    Section __text: 3440
    Section __stubs: 216
    Section __gcc_except_tab: 108
    Section __cstring: 95
    Section __unwind_info: 256
    total 4115
Segment __DATA_CONST: 16384
    Section __got: 168
    total 168
Segment __DATA: 4014080
    Section __data: 16
    Section __common: 4000000 (zerofill)
    total 4000016
Segment __LINKEDIT: 16384
total 4299030528
$ nm segments | grep -E '_g_|lastTick|where|_main$'
00000001000005d8 T __Z5wherePKv
00000001000005d0 T __Z8lastTickv
0000000100008010 S _g_book
0000000100008000 D _g_orders
0000000100008008 D _g_venue
00000001000005ec T _main
```

macOS names the sections its own way: `__text` is text, `__cstring` holds the literals, `__data` is data, and `__common` holds zero-filled globals. A read-only table goes in `__const`, the kind of read-only data where *const, constexpr, and Where a Value Lives* counted a `constexpr` fee table, one copy per file, or one in all when it's `inline`, and a constant the compiler folds into the instructions never reaches a segment at all. Three things to read off this program:

- `g_book` is 4 MB of zeros, marked zerofill. The file only records its size, and the OS hands the program zeroed pages when it starts, so the whole program is 55816 bytes. Give the array one value, `= {1}`, and it moves to `__data` and the file grows to 4085224 bytes.
- `nm` marks code `T` and data `D`, and `S` is another section. Each name starts with an underscore on macOS, and `__Z8lastTickv` is `lastTick()` mangled.
- `__PAGEZERO` reserves the first 4 GB of addresses with nothing in them. Any access there crashes at once, which is why dereferencing `nullptr` crashes instead of reading garbage.

On Linux, `size a.out` prints the text, data, and bss sizes, `readelf -S a.out` lists the sections (`.text`, `.rodata`, `.data`, `.bss`), `nm` marks rodata `R` and bss `B`, and `cat /proc/self/maps` run inside a program shows its live regions. With MSVC, `dumpbin /headers` lists `.text`, `.rdata`, and `.data`.

example.title: Which region is lower
example.prompt: Compare the addresses of a function, a string literal, two globals, a heap int, and a local to see the order of the segments, then read a global that was never set.
example.output:
text < rodata: true
rodata < data: true
data < bss: true
bss < heap: true
heap < stack: true
g_book[999999]: 0
example.explanation: A `const void*` parameter accepts a pointer to anything, and `where` turns it into a plain number with `reinterpret_cast`, so addresses from different regions can be compared with `<`. C++ promises no answer for comparing unrelated pointers directly, but numbers always compare. `&lastTick` is the address of the function's machine code. Each line compares two neighbors from the table, and every one is true: code at the bottom, then the literal, the data, the 4 MB of bss, the heap, and the stack near the top. Only the comparisons print, since the addresses themselves change from run to run. `g_book[999999]` is 0 although nothing wrote it, because every global and static starts zeroed. A local array gets no such promise.

practice.title: Below the heap or above it
practice.prompt:
Find out which side of the heap each kind of variable lives on.

1. The starter's `new int(7)` is the heap marker, `order`. For `kLimits`, `g_fills`, the static `calls` (its address is what `callCounter()` returns), the local `prices`, and the literal `"XNAS"`, print `<name> below heap: ` followed by whether its address is below the marker's, compared with `where`.
2. Then print `g_fills[49999]: ` followed by that element.

Expected output:

```text
kLimits below heap: true
g_fills below heap: true
calls below heap: true
prices below heap: false
XNAS below heap: true
g_fills[49999]: 0
```

tests.output:
kLimits below heap: true
g_fills below heap: true
calls below heap: true
prices below heap: false
XNAS below heap: true
g_fills[49999]: 0

hints: `callCounter()` returns `&calls`, so `where(callCounter())` is the static's address.
Only `prices` is on the stack, and the stack sits above the heap.

steps.title: Four storage durations

example.title: Watching objects come and go
example.prompt: Make a global, a local, a heap object, and a static and an automatic local in a function called twice, all of a type that prints when each is made and destroyed.
example.output:
make global config
main starts
make session
make cache
make static book
make tick scratch
drop tick scratch
make tick scratch
drop tick scratch
drop cache
main ends
drop session
drop static book
drop global config
example.explanation: `g_config` is static, so it's made before `main` prints anything and destroyed last of all. `session` is automatic and lives until `main`'s closing brace. `cache` is dynamic: made at `new`, dropped at `delete`, wherever those are. In `handleTick`, the static `book` is made on the first call only, while `scratch` is made and dropped on every call. After `main ends`, `session` goes at the brace, then the statics in the reverse of their making: `book`, made later, before `g_config`.

practice.title: Order of life and death
practice.prompt:
Place a probe of each storage duration and match the order they print in.

1. In `sendOrder`, add a static `Noisy` named `order log`, then an automatic one named `order message`.
2. In `main`, after `main starts`, make an automatic `Noisy` named `risk limits`.
3. Open an inner block holding a `Noisy` named `quote`, and print `block ends` just before its closing brace.
4. Make a `Noisy` named `snapshot` with `new`, call `sendOrder()` twice, then `delete` the snapshot.

Expected output:

```text
make price feed
main starts
make risk limits
make quote
block ends
drop quote
make snapshot
make order log
make order message
drop order message
make order message
drop order message
drop snapshot
main ends
drop risk limits
drop order log
drop price feed
```

tests.output:
make price feed
main starts
make risk limits
make quote
block ends
drop quote
make snapshot
make order log
make order message
drop order message
make order message
drop order message
drop snapshot
main ends
drop risk limits
drop order log
drop price feed

hints: `static Noisy log("order log");` is made on the first call only.
`quote` is dropped at its block's closing brace, right after `block ends`.
`Noisy* snapshot = new Noisy("snapshot");` and later `delete snapshot;`.

steps.title: The static initialization order problem

example.title: Read before it's set
example.prompt: In one file, read a global from an earlier global's initializer before it's set, then fix it with a function that holds the value in a static local.
example.output:
loading tick size
loading tick size
main starts
seen at start: 0
now: 5
fixed: 5 5
example.explanation: Both `loading tick size` lines print before `main starts`, since globals are set before `main` runs. `g_seenAtStart` is declared first, so its initializer runs first and calls `readTickSize()` while `g_tickSize` still holds the zero every static starts with. Only then does `g_tickSize` get its 5. `tickSize()` has no such problem: the first call, from the initializer of `g_fixedAtStart`, runs `loadTickSize()` and sets `size`, and every later call returns that same `int` through the reference. In a real program the function replaces the global. Here both stay so you can compare them.

practice.title: A lot size that's ready in time
practice.prompt:
Fix a global that's read before it's set by holding its value in a static local.

1. Replace the global `g_lotSize` with a function `int& lotSize()` that holds `static int size = loadLotSize();` and returns it.
2. Make `readLotSize()` return `lotSize()`.
3. Leave `g_lotsAtStart` where it is.

Expected output:

```text
loading lot size
main starts
lot size at start: 100
lot size now: 100
```

tests.output:
loading lot size
main starts
lot size at start: 100
lot size now: 100

hints: Delete the line `int g_lotSize = loadLotSize();` and write the function in its place, above `readLotSize()`.
The function's body is two lines: the `static int` and `return size;`.
`loading lot size` prints once, because the static local is set only on the first call.

steps.title: Stack limits and where new gets memory

example.title: Three sizes, two system calls
example.prompt: Allocate 1000, 10^5, and 10^6 bytes with new[] and use glibc's own counters to see which came from memory malloc already had, which grew the heap, and which got a mapping of its own.
example.output:
heap in use before main: yes
1000 bytes: from the heap malloc already had
100000 bytes: the heap grew (brk)
1000000 bytes: a mapping of its own (mmap)
mapped blocks after delete[]: 0
example.explanation: `mallinfo()` is glibc's report on itself: its `arena` field counts the heap's bytes, and `hblks` the blocks that got their own `mmap`. The heap is in use before `main`, 135168 bytes here, because the C++ runtime allocated while the program started. 1000 bytes fit in its free space, so neither counter moved. 100000 bytes didn't fit, so `malloc` grew the heap with `brk`, by more than it needed, 176128 bytes here, to leave room for the next requests. The program prints which way each request went, not the byte counts, which change with the C library's version and settings. 10^6 bytes is over 128 KB, so it got a mapping of its own, and `delete[]` gave it back at once, taking the count to 0. `<malloc.h>` and `mallinfo` are Linux only, so this program won't build on the Mac.

practice.title: Where each allocation comes from
practice.prompt:
Write the function that reports where an allocation came from, and run it on three sizes.

1. Write `char* allocate(long n)` that reads `heapBytes()` and `mappedBlocks()`, allocates `n` bytes with `new char[n]`, and returns the block.
2. Before it returns, it prints `<n> bytes: a mapping of its own (mmap)` if `mappedBlocks()` went up, else `<n> bytes: the heap grew (brk)` if `heapBytes()` went up, else `<n> bytes: from the heap malloc already had`.
3. In `main`, allocate `64`, `80'000`, and `300'000` bytes in that order, then `delete[]` all three.

Expected output:

```text
64 bytes: from the heap malloc already had
80000 bytes: the heap grew (brk)
300000 bytes: a mapping of its own (mmap)
mapped blocks after delete[]: 0
```

tests.output:
64 bytes: from the heap malloc already had
80000 bytes: the heap grew (brk)
300000 bytes: a mapping of its own (mmap)
mapped blocks after delete[]: 0

hints: Read both counters into locals before `new char[n]`, then compare them with fresh calls after it.
Check `mappedBlocks()` first: an mmap block doesn't change `heapBytes()`.
Free each block with `delete[]`, since it came from `new[]`.

recap:
- A process has its own virtual address space, laid out as text, rodata, data, bss, heap, and stack, from low addresses to high.
- bss takes no room in the program file, since its pages arrive zeroed. `size -m` and `nm` show the segments and symbols on the Mac, `size`, `readelf -S`, and `nm` on Linux.
- Every global and static starts at zero. A local gets no such promise.
- Automatic objects live to their closing brace, statics from before `main` to after it (destroyed newest first), `thread_local` ones once per thread, and dynamic ones from `new` to `delete`, or forever if leaked.
- A static local is made the first time its function runs, safely even with threads.
- Globals in different files are set in an unspecified order. Hold such a value in a static local, or make it `constexpr`.
- The main thread's stack is 8 MB here and on the Mac. Too deep a recursion overflows it, with exit status 139.
- `new` calls `malloc`, which grows the heap with `brk` or maps big blocks with `mmap`, both trips to the kernel.

Next, **Memory Hierarchy: Registers, Caches, RAM, Pages, and Disk** follows those virtual addresses down to real memory: the registers, the caches, the pages, and the disk.
